newsitem.title: GERMANY: Reinsurers take break from mega deals-industry.
newsitem.headline: Reinsurers take break from mega deals-industry.

text.p: Reinsurers gathered to discuss the upcoming renewals season said on Wednesday further large-scale acquisitions and mergers were unlikely in the near term, particularly in Europe, after a wave of takeover activity during the summer.
"As far as Germany and Europe are concerned, the takeovers (among reinsurers) have come to an end for the time being," Colonia Konzern AG board member Axel Biagosch told Reuters.

Big deals in recent months included Swiss Re's acquisition of M&G Re, Munich Re's purchase of American Re and General Re's move on National Reinsurance, as well as a joint venture deal involving Colonia itself.

"When we started our joint venture with General Re and brought Koelnische Rueck into this venture it was the very first of these mega deals...We did not know that we were starting an avalanche," the Colonia director said.
CKAG, which is majority owned by UAP, does a limited amount of organising for the largely informal get-together of reinsurers in Baden-Baden every October.
The meeting, which continues until Friday, signals the start of detailed negotiations for the renewal of major reinsurance contracts in January.
Biagosch said consolidation would continue among small and medium sized insurers, as well as primary insurers.
"Companies of a relatively small size will not be able to survive and therefore there will be a process of smaller mergers by smaller units."
Industry sources said there was also room for some niche reinsurers alongside the big groups, but agreed that otherwise there was little prospect of smaller players surviving.
"Clients are interested in good security and strong capitalisation," one German reinsurer said.
Biagosch said the process of consolidation would be driven by insurance becoming more technical and complex, making it too costly for small operators to succeed.

Only large companies could afford the central services, information technology and risk transfer systems necessary to survive in an increasingly competitive and demanding market, industry representatives said.
Pressures would also increase on insurers and reinsurers to reduce costs.
"We must desperately try to bring our costs down and this can only be done by greater units," said Biagosch.
Clients would no longer tolerate the current cost ratios of 28-30 percent, which Biagosch believes can be cut by around five percent over the next three years.
"If it is not done over the next three years, it will probably be extremely difficult to do later," he added.
